title: Removes Geoffrey Berman as U.S. Attorney
description_medium: In June 2020, Attorney General William Barr announced that Geoffrey Berman would leave as U.S. attorney for Manhattan, but Berman publicly said he had not resigned and would stay until a successor was confirmed. Barr then said Trump had approved Berman’s removal. Berman’s office oversaw sensitive investigations, including cases involving Trump associates; he left after a weekend standoff.
description_long:
Geoffrey Berman led the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York, a high-profile federal prosecutor’s office whose investigations included cases involving President Trump’s former lawyer Michael Cohen and associates of Rudy Giuliani. On June 19, 2020, Attorney General William Barr announced that Berman was “stepping down” and that Trump planned to nominate Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Jay Clayton to replace him. Berman immediately disputed the announcement, saying he had not resigned and would remain until a Senate-confirmed successor took office.

The standoff became public that night. Barr wrote to Berman the next day that he had asked Trump to remove him and that Trump had done so. Berman then agreed to leave after Barr assured him that Deputy U.S. Attorney Audrey Strauss would continue leading the office. Berman said he wanted the office’s investigations to proceed without interruption. Trump publicly said he had not been involved, while Barr said the president had approved the removal. The abrupt effort to replace a court-appointed prosecutor prompted questions about the Justice Department’s independence, especially because the office was pursuing matters involving people close to the president. The record establishes the unusual public dispute and departure; claims about a motive require attribution rather than assumption.

corrected_wording.original: Forces Out U.S. Attorney Geoffrey Berman
corrected_wording.replacement: Removes Geoffrey Berman as U.S. Attorney
corrected_wording.reason: The revision describes the documented removal without treating the public standoff as evidence of a specific motive.

source_access_notes: Read Berman’s June 19 DOJ statement, contemporaneous CBS reporting and the Washington Post account of his later congressional testimony. The supplied Time path was unavailable; these sources cover the same removal and standoff.
rationale: DOJ records Berman’s refusal to resign and stated intention to protect case continuity; contemporaneous reporting establishes Barr’s removal request, Trump’s role and the interim succession.

title: Fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper
description_medium: On November 9, 2020, six days after the presidential election, Donald Trump announced that Defense Secretary Mark Esper had been terminated and installed Christopher Miller as acting secretary. Esper had publicly opposed invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy active-duty troops against racial-justice protesters. The abrupt change came during the presidential transition and placed a new leader atop the Pentagon in Trump’s final months.
description_long:
Trump fired Esper by tweet on November 9, 2020, less than a week after the presidential election. He said Christopher Miller, then director of the National Counterterrorism Center, would become acting secretary of defense immediately. The choice bypassed Deputy Defense Secretary David Norquist, the department’s second-ranking official. Esper had learned of his dismissal shortly before Trump’s post, according to a defense official quoted by CBS News.

The firing followed months of tension over the role of the military in domestic law enforcement. During protests after George Floyd’s killing, Trump threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act and deploy active-duty troops. Esper publicly said the law should be used only in the most urgent and dire situations and that the country was not in such a situation. He and Joint Chiefs Chairman Mark Milley had also resisted a reported demand for 10,000 active-duty troops. Trump’s action came amid his refusal to accept defeat in the election and raised questions about continuity and civilian control during the transition. Esper’s letter to the Defense Department emphasized keeping the armed forces apolitical; Democrats criticized the timing and described the removal as destabilizing. The immediate appointment of an acting secretary ensured the department remained under civilian leadership, but created uncertainty about the transition.
source_access_notes: Read CBS’s same-day coverage of the firing and Insurrection Act dispute. PBS/AP and the Guardian provide corroborating same-event reports; the packet’s Guardian endpoint was inaccessible, so the corrected Guardian page was used.
rationale: Contemporaneous coverage documents the tweet, acting successor and public disagreement over deploying active-duty forces; claims about retaliatory motive remain attributed to political critics.

title: Pardons Rick Renzi
description_medium: On January 20, 2021, President Donald Trump granted former Arizona Representative Rick Renzi a full pardon, four years after Renzi left prison. Renzi had served nearly two years of a 36-month federal sentence after a jury convicted him of public-corruption, racketeering, fraud and money-laundering offenses. The White House highlighted his three House terms and supporters’ claims about his constituent service; Republican lawmakers had advocated for clemency.
description_long:
Rick Renzi represented Arizona in the U.S. House from 2003 to 2009. A federal jury convicted him in 2013 of 17 counts, including extortion, bribery, insurance fraud, money laundering and racketeering. Prosecutors said Renzi used his office in a proposed copper-mine land swap to benefit a former business associate who owed him money. The jury also found that Renzi had committed insurance-related fraud. Renzi denied wrongdoing, and his convictions were upheld on appeal. He was sentenced to 36 months in prison, three years of supervised release and a $25,000 fine; he left prison in January 2017.

Trump granted Renzi a full pardon on January 20, 2021, in the final clemency announcements of his presidency. The White House cited Renzi’s three terms in Congress and said constituents regarded him as an advocate for housing, education and health care. It listed support from Representative Paul Gosar, several former Republican House members and community supporters. The pardon came years after Renzi had completed his prison term, though it did not erase the historical conviction. The case drew attention because an elected official convicted of abusing public office received clemency after political colleagues publicly backed him. The grant itself does not establish an improper exchange.
source_access_notes: Read the DOJ clemency table, White House January 20 announcement, AP’s same-day account and Cronkite News’ case reporting. They establish offense, sentence, appeal, pardon and listed supporters.
rationale: DOJ and contemporaneous reporting establish the convictions, sentence and grant. The White House supplies its stated positive rationale and supporters; the prose avoids asserting an unproven exchange.

title: Pardons Peter Y. Atkinson
description_medium: President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Peter Y. Atkinson on December 23, 2020. Atkinson, a former Hollinger International vice president, had served 345 days in prison for three mail-fraud counts arising from the company’s fraud scheme and received three years of supervised release and a $3,000 fine. The White House cited his service and support from former Hollinger owner Conrad Black.
description_long:
Peter Y. Atkinson was a vice president of Hollinger International, the newspaper company led by Conrad Black. Federal prosecutors accused Black and other executives of diverting company funds through unauthorized payments and related fraud; Atkinson was convicted of three mail-fraud counts. The Justice Department’s clemency record lists a sentence of 345 days in prison, which he had already served, three years of supervised release and a $3,000 fine. The sentencing date shown in that record is December 2007; it is not the date of Trump’s later pardon.

On December 23, 2020, Trump granted Atkinson a full pardon alongside former Hollinger chief financial officer John Boultbee. The White House described both men as convicted in an alleged fraud scheme involving Black, said they had each served nearly a year for mail fraud, and noted that Trump had pardoned Black the previous year. It said Atkinson’s pardon was granted for similar reasons and with Black’s support, alongside support from former attorneys general and other former Justice Department officials. The account links the pardon to advocacy by a prominent earlier clemency recipient. The pardon did not itself establish that Atkinson’s conviction was wrongful or erase the historical case.
source_access_notes: Read DOJ’s clemency list and the White House’s December 23, 2020 announcement. The White House identifies Atkinson’s Hollinger role, prior sentence, supporters and the relationship to Conrad Black’s earlier pardon.
rationale: The DOJ table supplies the conviction and sentence date; the White House establishes the actual pardon date and stated rationale. The prose distinguishes sentencing date from clemency date.

title: Pardons Andrew Barron Worden
description_medium: President Donald Trump granted Andrew Barron Worden a full pardon on December 23, 2020, for a 1995 wire-fraud conviction. The White House said Worden had just graduated from college when he made mistakes managing an investment firm, then stopped the conduct and began repaying victims before criminal charges were filed. It cited his later solar-energy work and philanthropy, while DOJ records the sentence as two years’ probation and ongoing SEC payments.
description_long:
Andrew Barron Worden was convicted of wire fraud in a 1995 federal case in the Southern District of New York. The Justice Department’s clemency table lists two years of probation, 100 hours of community service each year and continued payment of the balance owed to the Securities and Exchange Commission. That date in the DOJ table refers to the underlying sentence, not the clemency action.

On December 23, 2020, Trump granted Worden a full pardon. The White House described him as a solar-energy entrepreneur and philanthropist and said he had recently graduated from college when he made mistakes running an investment firm. Its announcement said Worden voluntarily stopped the conduct and began repaying victims before criminal charges were filed; it quoted the sentencing judge calling that repayment “extraordinary.” Business associates and community members supported the pardon. The administration’s account offered rehabilitation and early repayment as reasons for clemency. The pardon covered the federal conviction, but the public statement and DOJ entry do not say that the pardon cancelled Worden’s remaining SEC payment obligation. The grant therefore merits description alongside the prior sentence and the administration’s stated rationale, without implying that the record proves corruption or a personal exchange.
source_access_notes: Read DOJ’s pardon table and the White House’s December 23 announcement, including its account of Worden’s repayment before charges and its description of the sentence and supporters.
rationale: DOJ establishes the offense and sentence; the White House fixes the pardon date and gives its stated rationale. The entry’s sentencing date is distinguished from the actual 2020 clemency date.
